Overview

Showing what the robot is doing

Orchestra Display was developed for a surgical assistant robot project under the Korean ARPA-H program. A tablet mounted on the robot’s head shows its current activity and recognized voice commands, using status updates from the robot’s operating software.

Software architecture · Robot integration

Separating robot control from the display

Robot actions remain in the existing control program. A separate API and display app receive state constants and the information needed on screen over the same network.

Add a status call when an action changes

Set the tablet’s address and robot ID once, then call the send function at action transitions in the existing program. This keeps integration work small: robot developers do not need to build the display or handle network communication themselves.

The scope assistant also uses an observer that reads the existing controller’s state and maps it to a display state. Each integration follows the robot’s actions without making the display app depend directly on its control logic.

Send updates in the background

A status call adds an event to a queue and returns. HTTP requests and retries run in the background, so the robot program does not wait for transmission to finish.

Check the integration and display without a robot

The instrument delivery and scope assistant modules include a receiver server that runs on a PC. The same status calls can be sent to the PC to inspect transmission logs, then redirected to the tablet to check the actual screens.

Changes on the robot side
Configure the connection and add status calls. The existing program still runs the actions and determines when they are complete.
Changes to the display
As long as the state definitions stay the same, text, icons and transitions can be revised within the display app.
What both sides agree on
State names and when to send them. Adding a state requires matching definitions in the robot program and display app.

A display for each robot

The Orchestra Display apps

Separate display apps were built for instrument delivery, scope assistance and teleoperation. Each has its own states and prompts, with screens tailored to the task.

August–September 2026 · States and screen copy

Mapping robot actions to states and prompts

The robot source code was reviewed to identify instrument search, grasp, handover, retrieval, movement and tracking actions. Display states and prompts were then defined for each stage.

Shorter prompts and clear icons help users recognize the current action. Screens were compared across states and refined to stay readable and transition smoothly as actions change.

The background and frame stay in place to avoid full-screen flashing. Titles, icons and prompts transition smoothly at fixed positions.

2026.09.12 · Display 1 v0.3.15

Instrument delivery states and voice commands

The app shows 19 states covering requests, preparation, handover, retrieval and return. The recognized voice command stays in the top card, with text sized to fit its length. The card height and text baseline remain fixed.

2026.09.14 · Display 2 v0.38.0

Clearer status and faster screen transitions

The app shows instrument movement, automatic tracking and return to the ready position. Movement and tracking states take priority, so incoming voice commands do not obscure an action already in progress.

State transitions on two screens were compared in a 136-second recording. Repeated queries for up to 500 database entries and a 70–80 ms wait before opening a new screen were removed. The completion screen now appears only after a completion event arrives.

Display 3 v0.5.6

Teleoperation status screens

The app shows waiting for connection, connecting, teleoperation, session ended and connection error states. A Python module on the robot PC sends status updates and keepalive signals; the app on a Lenovo Y700 displays the corresponding screen.
